speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: FOOD FOR PEACE CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 17 I made a statement about the forthcoming food for peace conference and stated that a little later I would place before the house the composition of the Canadian delegation.
This ministerial meeting will take place in Washington on the 4th and 5th of May and the Canadian government will be represented by the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Agriculture. The delegation will also include Mr. McNamara, chief commissioner of the wheat board, and government officials from the departments of trade and commerce, finance, agriculture and external affairs, as well as from the Canadian embassy in Washington.
The chairman of the Canadian delegation to the meeting of officials which is now taking place in Washington is Mr. G. R. Paterson, chief of the agricultural and fisheries branch of the Department of Trade and Commerce, who will be assisted by officials of the departments concerned, the wheat board and the Canadian embassy in Washington.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: STATEMENT ON CANADA'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 22 I gave the house an account of the stage that had been reached in the preparations by the four western powers for the negotiations with the Soviet union which are to commence in Geneva on May 11. I mentioned on that occasion that a committee of experts from the United States, the United Kingdom, France and West Germany was engaged in compiling draft proposals for the western side. That work has been completed.
Yesterday in the United Kingdom House of Commons the foreign secretary, Mr. Lloyd, gave an account of the hopes and expectations for the Geneva meeting. It is apparent from a reading of his speech that as yet it has not been found possible to go
into detail about the exact negotiating position of the western countries. However, Mr. Lloyd was able to say enough to show that the United Kingdom, in its thinking on the problems to be examined in Geneva, is following much the same viewpoint as that expressed on behalf of the Canadian government. We have been aware of the similarity of our views as a result of discussions with the United Kingdom Prime Minister and Mr. Lloyd when they were in Ottawa recently.
Specifically, the Canadian government is associated in public, as it has already been in private, with the United Kingdom belief in the need for real negotiations, and we give complete support to the three major aims which Mr. Lloyd set forth. The western powers should try to achieve some progress first toward the reunification of Germany on acceptable terms. Canada reaffirms the right of the people of West Berlin to choose their own system of society along with satisfactory arrangements for free access to that city. As well, there should be a reduction in tension and an improvement of stability in Europe.
These three aims represent in general the viewpoint expressed by Mr. Lloyd. There are formidable difficulties in the way of achieving them. It may turn out that the foreign ministers' conference at Geneva and the summit meeting which it is expected will follow may be but the beginning of a series of consultations with the Soviet union on these vital problems. That in itself would be an advance. As the western foreign ministers are about to begin the final preparations I think the house would want me to assure them that they have the full understanding of this house and of the Canadian people in the task that faces them.

Representing the province of Nova Scotia were Premier Robert L. Stanfield and Hon. E. A. Manson, minister of mines, who met with the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys, the Minister of National Revenue and Mr. Wilbur Uren, chairman of the dominion coal board.

speechtext:
I would like to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, notice of which I sent to his office at 11.45 this forenoon. In view of recent action by the government of Jamaica in placing a low ceiling of 13J cents at the retail level on dry pollock, and this

at a time when Canadian exporters have over 4 million pounds of this commodity on hand, what action, if any, is being taken by the government to protect this market for our Canadian producers?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: REPORTED CEILING PRICE SET BY JAMAICA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, notice of the question of the hon. member was duly received at 11.45 a.m. The answer had already been prepared, because a week ago we were aware of this situation. On April 21 we were advised of the Jamaican government's intention to place a retail price ceiling of one shilling per pound on dry salted pollock. Immediately on receipt of this information our trade commissioner in Jamaica was instructed to make strong representations to the Jamaican authorities. The trade commissioner has now advised us that effective April 27 the retail price ceiling on dry salt pollock has been removed.
It is my understanding that the Jamaican minister of trade and industry will be meeting tomorrow with fish importers in Jamaica to work out new conditions covering the importation of salt fish. I can assure the house that the strongest representations will be made by our trade commissioner in Jamaica to ensure that Canadian exporters continue to enjoy favourable terms of access to this important and traditional market. It would be unfortunate if discriminatory action were taken by the Jamaican authorities which would lead in any way to a deterioration in the close and friendly relations between Canada and Jamaica.

In view of the fact that the Dominion Steel and Coal Company have announced that they will be closing down No. 6 mine at Bell Island on May 1, thereby placing 575 miners out of work, would the minister tell the house what steps have been taken to meet this situation?
Further, is the minister prepared' to say whether consideration will be given to declaring Bell Island a labour surplus area, thereby making it possible for financial assistance to be given to those miners to secure work elsewhere?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: BELL ISLAND, NFLD.    ASSISTANCE TO UNEMPLOYED MINERS
speechtext:
I wish to thank the hon. member for having given me notice of this question. My department has been very active in attempting to ease the situation of those affected by this lay-off. given regarding the movement of tough and damp grain in the northeastern corner of Saskatchewan?
Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade
and Commerce): Yes, Mr. Speaker. This is a matter which is of considerable concern to the producers of that area, and every effort has been made to meet their requirements. The wheat board has advised me now that while very little space is available for local deliveries at the points in northeastern Saskatchewan which are affected, there are outstanding shipping orders in the hands of the elevator agents for 30 cars, 12 cars and 15 cars, respectively, for three areas, Hudson Bay, Veillardville and Erwood. As navigation at the lakehead has just opened, grain to that destination will be moving more freely from now on, and it is anticipated by the Canadian wheat board that the railway company will be in a position to furnish box cars in fulfilment of the outstanding orders and additional orders commencing within a few days. As space becomes available for further deliveries by producers, delivery quotas will be increased accordingly.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the course of my brief introductory remarks last evening I laid some emphasis on one or two points. The first was in reference to the bank rate, 66968-9-1974
Monetary Policy
that is to say the Bank of Canada rate. I had pointed out that that is a rate established by the Bank of Canada under the provisions of the Bank of Canada Act, and the government has no power over the rate that is established by the Bank of Canada. I had given some indication, Mr. Speaker, of what I think is a fairly widely recognized fact, that in Canada and some other countries with relatively new central banks the bank rate, that is to say the rate established by the central bank only, has exerted no direct or strong influence on market rates. Its movement has rather reflected changes in market rates and market conditions, and could never have been properly considered a cause of those rates and conditions.
I had also pointed, Mr. Speaker, to the fluctuations that have occurred in various rates. I had pointed out that in this country the rise in interest rates began not recently but in 1955, and that in the summer of 1957 a decline in interest rates set in which lasted for nearly a year, until the spring of 1958. We have been, since that time, in a period of rising interest rates in company with some other countries.
I pointed out also, Mr. Speaker, the extent to which the prime rate established by the chartered banks of Canada has fluctuated. I pointed out that the rise to 5J per cent which became effective yesterday simply returned that rate to the figure it had reached at the peak of the movement in interest rates in the summer of 1957, climaxing at that time a rise in interest rates that had then continued, broadly speaking, for two and one half years.
I am sure I do not need to say to the house that the government has no jurisdiction whatever over the prime rate established by the chartered banks. Section 91 of the Bank Act is quite clear in its provisions in this regard. It prohibits the banks from charging any rate of interest or any rate of discount exceeding 6 per cent per annum. It does not give the government any power whatever over the rate established by the banks. Therefore in pointing to that rate hon. members in the opposition who have sought to make something of it are simply pointing to something over which the government has been given no jurisdiction or measure of control by parliament.
Now, sir, having mentioned these points again, let me pass on to further observations on the theme upon which I touched last night, as to the effect of the operation of the law of supply and demand in the money market. I had indicated that when this law is left alone it operates in the same way the law of supply and demand operates in the-commodity markets. When the supply factors are stronger than the demand factors,,

Monetary Policy
then obviously the price goes down, in this case interest rates. On the other hand, when the demand factors are in the ascendant over the supply factors, then the price goes up, in this case the price of money being interest.
One would have thought, sir, listening to the speeches that were made by opposition members yesterday, that something extraordinary had happened, something that was quite unprecedented. Well, Mr. Speaker, the fact is that hon. members opposite, as I pointed out last night, chose for their favourite illustration the treasury bill rate, which is the rate which has shown, in the period from the summer of 1957 to the spring of 1958, the sharpest drop in interest rates and since that time the sharpest rise. It is the most volatile of all government securities in its response to factors at work in the market affecting interest rates. One does not find in the case of any of the government bond issues movements in interest rates to compare with those which did occur in those two periods in the treasury bill rate.
I could give the house detailed figures, but I do not wish to weary the house. However, whether one looks at short, medium or long term bonds, the fact is that in one of these cases have the movements in interest rates been as sharp as in the case of treasury bills, and that is obviously the reason hon. members of the opposition, in seeking to exaggerate this situation out of all recognition, have chosen to talk about the treasury bill rate and have completely glossed over the position in regard to bonds. The fact is also that hon. members of the opposition, in speaking yesterday left the impression that this situation is confined to our country. I am sure the house is not going to be so easily misled. We are, in this respect, experiencing a problem that is shared with other countries.
I gave the figures last night showing the rise in the treasury bill rate. Let us look at the United States. One hon. member opposite yesterday pictured the United States as enjoying reduced rates on its borrowings. Well, Mr. Speaker, here are the figures on United States treasury bills, beginning with the first of this year. The opening rate on a treasury bill issue of the United States for this year, January 7, was 2.68 per cent. Their last offering, on April 22, went out at 3.11 per cent.
The rise, as hon. members will see, was .43 per cent, and that condition has been similar to the one we find in the United Kingdom. Basic conditions in the United Kingdom may be somewhat different at present from those on this continent, but with respect to the treasury bill rate we see,

though not to the same extent, nevertheless the same general condition. The opening treasury bill rate in the United Kingdom this year, on January 7, was 3.14 per cent. The last issue, on April 22, went out at 3.28 per cent. This rise is smaller, it is true, nevertheless it is a rise.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the rate in Canada on treasury bills has, in its movements, paralleled the movements that have occurred in other countries. If the treasury bill rate, which is only one rate, has moved farther in this period than in these other countries, there are good reasons for it, and I think reasons that commend themselves to this house and to the country. I point out also that much sharper rises than we have experienced in this country in our treasury bill rate have occurred in other countries. Look at the experience in the United Kingdom in 1957. On July 31, the treasury bill rate in that country was 3.82 per cent, and by September 25 the rate had jumped to 6.6 per cent.
When hon. members opposite talk about the jump in our rate, it would be well if these things were seen in their true perspective. The fact is that the treasury bill rate in this country, since the beginning of 1959, has jumped just 1.47 per cent. We are not at all happy that this increase has occurred but, Mr. Speaker, it is well, in all honesty, that the facts should be understood and that the kind of misleading impression that was created yesterday should not be permitted to linger. I have indicated also that when the treasury bill rate recedes, we derive immediate benefit from the reduction because of the weekly offerings.
Now, sir, we are told that we have influenced rates on bonds and on treasury bills. It is undoubtedly a fact, Mr. Speaker, that a government would like to affect those rates to its advantages as it may be able. No government likes to pay more than it must for the money it must borrow to meet the purposes of government. What has been our record, Mr. Speaker? Our record has been this. In the matter of issuance of bonds we have taken advantage of the decline in interest rates which, as I pointed out, set in in the summer of 1957, and we took advantage of that right through until the rate began to rise again in the late spring of 1958.
Here have been our issues, Mr. Speaker, and I give the effective rates. On October 1, 1957, we put out an issue of $400 million of 3 per cent short term bonds, and the effective rate was 4.81 per cent. On the same date we also put out $300 million of two year bonds with an effective rate of 4.99 per cent. Note, Mr. Speaker, what had happened by the time the next issue was put out; already the interest rate had declined. On December 15,

1957	we put out an issue of $250 million of 3 per cent, approximately two year bonds at a rate of 3.81 per cent. Between October 1 and December 15 our borrowing rate on these two year bonds had declined by over 1 per cent. We also put out on December 15 a 3 per cent issue of longer term bonds maturing in 1960 carrying a yield of 3.85 per cent.
By May of 1958 interest rates had declined still further, and we were able to take advantage of that decline. On May 1 we put out four issues totalling $950 million, the maturities falling due in 1959, 1961, 1970 and 1978, and the actual yields to final maturity respectively were 2.94 per cent, 3.35 per cent, 3.71 per cent and 4.01 per cent.
The house will see, Mr. Speaker, that in that very substantial issue of $950 million we were enjoying the benefit of the decline in interest rates. It is also an illustration of the fact that the preference of the market at that time was for the shorter maturities, and we were able to borrow in the shorter range at substantially lower rates than in the longest maturity.
Then we move forward to July 15. We issued another $400 million on July 15 maturing at the end of 1958, and they were put out at a rate of 2J per cent. I will pass over the conversion loans for the present because I will be coming back to them later. On October 1 we put out two issues aggregating $600 million, these maturing in 1959 and 1960 respectively. Here the yield to maturity was 2.77 per cent and 2.96 per cent respectively. The house will see what advantage we were enjoying from the decline in interest rates.
Then on December 15 we put out a loan of $300 million maturing at the end of 1959, at a rate of 3.77 per cent. In the fall of
1958	interest rates, in response to conditions about which I shall have something more to say, had begun to rise. That rise continued into 1959, as the house well knows. On January 1 we put out an issue of $100 million maturing in 1963 at an effective rate of 4.34 per cent. On March 1 we put out two issues totalling $200 million, both maturing in 1960, one in April and the other in December, the effective yield to maturity being 4.76 per cent and 4.94 per cent respectively.
It is well, I think, that these facts should be placed on the record to correct the misleading impression that was created yesterday by hon. members opposite. They have taken no little satisfaction in their speeches over the fact that interest rates have risen in recent months. They seem to gloat and glory in the fact that interest rates have risen and
Monetary Policy
that the government, like every other borrower in Canada, has had to pay higher interest rates. Where were these voluble members a year ago, Mr. Speaker? Where were they with their speeches in the days when interest rates were receding and the government was enjoying in its borrowings the advantage of these substantially lower interest rates? Did we hear talk from them then about the strength the government had imparted to confidence in Canada? Oh, no, not these hon. members; no, they save what they have to say on the subject for the days when they can gloat and glory in the higher cost that the government, along with every other borrower in Canada, has to pay under the conditions that exist today. Such is the test, such is the mark of their sense of responsibility to Canada.
Let me address myself now, Mr. Speaker, to the situation which has been created today in which all borrowers have had to face higher interest charges. The situation we have today is a striking reflection of the operation of the forces of supply and demand in the economy, and it is a very interesting reflection of the strength of the expansive forces in the economy today. When we are asking these questions about the respective strengths of the forces of supply and demand in the money market I suggest that we begin with demand, and then I shall have something to say about supply.
On the demand side the most striking force at work in our economy in these recent times has been the strength of the recovery in the Canadian economy and the expansion of the forces of recovery at work in the Canadian economy at the present time. I do not expect hon. members opposite to like that fact.
It is not true.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They just do not like any talk about recovery in the Canadian economy-
Nonsense.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
-and they did not have the fairness yesterday to bring this factor into the discussion. In that way they gloss completely over the most important factor at work today influencing the relative play of the forces of supply and demand.
How is demand evidenced? Demand is evidenced in a very striking way, in bank loans. The banks do not hold their funds idle. They seek to employ them; and in order to keep their funds as liquid as possible they invest them in government of Canada bonds and in treasury bills, depending upon when they desire their maturities in the interests of liquidity.

Monetary Policy
Elementary, my dear Watson.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If it is elementary,
I have had to resort to elementary approaches for the benefit of hon. members opposite, to put a stop to the way they have been trying to mislead the house and the country on this issue.
Why don't you tell us about your big deficits?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I say, Mr. Speaker, that the banks of Canada have been called upon to meet an extraordinary demand for bank loans. The situation has attracted widespread attention in recent times. Mr. Speaker, here are the figures of loans of the chartered banks in recent weeks. At the beginning of this year the total of chartered bank loans was $5,402 million. By April 15 that figure had jumped to $5,658 million. Sir, that is an increase in bank loans of $256 million since the beginning of this year, 1959. And look, sir, if you will, at the way in which this increase has occurred. On April 1 the total of these loans outstanding was $5,528 million. Within a week

and I pointed this out a week ago in my speech-by April 8 that total had jumped to $5,629 million; that is an increase of $101 million in bank loans in one week. The following week, Mr. Speaker, by April 15 a jump of another $29 million occurred in outstanding bank loans.
Mr. Speaker, having regard to the function of the banks in our system, to provide credit to meet commercial necessities, we see mirrored in these figures of bank loans the extent to which recovery is going on in the Canadian ecoonmy today. It is going on at an extraordinary rate.
Would the minister permit a question? Could he give the comparable figures for the same months in 1957 and 1956?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I can give them for 1957 and 1958, if my hon. friend will be content with those.
Quite.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In 1957 the total of bank loans at the commencement of the year was $5,411 million. At April 22 it was $5,448 million. The rise in 1957 was only $37 million. Let us move forward to 1958. The total of bank loans outstanding at the opening of the year 1958 was $5,405 million. At April 22 it was $5,247 million. It had contracted in those first four months of 1958 by $158 million whereas, as I have pointed out to you, Mr. Speaker, in this year, 1959, the expansion in the total of bank loans has been $256 million. I appreciate my hon.

friend asking that question, because it gives me the opportunity of bringing out that interesting contrast which so clearly illustrates the extent of recovery of the economy of the country this year as compared with the conditions of a year ago.
Would the minister permit one further question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If the hon. member will ask another like the last one I would be delighted.

It is in fact almost exactly like the last one. Could the minister give for those same three years the demands which the government has made in the way of loans, just in order to illustrate this factor of demand? I want the amount which the government has borrowed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have already given the figure of demand in terms of all of the issues of government bonds by this government since it came into office in the summer of 1957.
But that does not answer my question.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I can go back and give the figures of issues of the government of which he was a member, if he has forgotten them. Perhaps he would like to forget that as well as some other features of the administration of his government.

I think the minister did not quite understand my question. I wanted the figures for precisely the same three months that the minister was using for purposes of illustration; that is to say, those issues between January 1 and April 22 for those three years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, I will be glad to get that information for my hon. friend, or any other information that will be of assistance to him.
Now, Mr. Speaker, how have the banks met this extraordinary demand for commercial loans? As I have said, the banks do not keep cash sitting idly around. They have to keep their money profitably employed. Just what happens in the face of an extraordinary demand like this on the banks? The fact is that the banks liquidate their holdings of securities in order to provide themselves with cash. The figures I am about to give the house now will illustrate the extent to which the banks have been realizing on their treasury bills, or taking their cash out of those bills as they mature week by week, and also reducing their holdings of government of Canada bonds by selling some of

these bonds in the market in order to put themselves in cash to meet this extraordinary demand for commercial loans. Here you have the reason why there has been pressure on the rate on treasury bills and the rate on government bonds in the market. It is because there has been selling by these institutions in order to put themselves in cash to meet the extraordinarily heavy demand for commercial loans arising out of the extent of recovery in this country.
Here are the figures. I do not wish to weary the house with a multitude of figures; perhaps it will suffice if I indicate to the house at this point the changes from week to week in the bank holdings of (a) bonds and (b) treasury bills, say from the beginning of February. Here are the figures, then, on bonds, showing the fluctuations from week to week. In the first week in February the banks showed an increase over the last week in January of $5 million in their total holdings of government of Canada bonds. The next week they were down $19 million. The next week they were about the same. The next week they were down $25 million. The next week they were up $41 million; the next week, down $4 million; the next week, up $16 million. Then, sir, will you note these next four weeks; down $15 million; down $19 million; down $57 million; down $54 million. If you wish to know why there has been pressure on the bond market and why this pressure has been reflected in rising interest rates, you have only to look at those figures of realizations by the chartered banks of their holdings of Dominion of Canada bonds.
Then let us look at the movement in their holdings of treasury bills; this is again for the same period. The first week in February showed an increase over the last week in January of $28 million. Then watch the next weeks. The second week, down $46 million; the next week, down $29 million; the next week, down $48 million; the next week, up $12 million; the next week, down $28 million; the next week, down $18 million; the next week, down $22 million; the next week, up $15 million; the next week, down $29 million; the next week, down $15 million.
Mr. Speaker, that succession of reductions illustrates as well as any figures can the essential facts in this situation, which are these. The banks have been liquidating their holdings of government bonds and treasury bills in order to put themselves in cash to meet the demands for commercial loans.

I wonder if the minister would clarify that point. Dealing with commercial loans he used a figure which, I take it, was based on the situation early in January, early in the year. He gave the composite figures, but in giving the holdings of
Monetary Policy
the chartered banks he started with the first week in February, which represented their peak over the last series of months. Is there any significance about not taking the corresponding dates for the two sets of figures?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Oh, no. I can go
on giving more figures if the house wishes them. The fact is that this significant reduction in the holdings of government of Canada bonds and treasury bills began at the end of the first week in February, and from that time on with only rare interruptions we have seen this process of liquidation continuing. The reason for this can be seen in the increase in the total number of bank loans outstanding, an increase which illustrates the extent of recovery in Canada.
This is again a reflection of the forces of supply and demand at work in the economy, and those hon. members of this house who are prepared to be fair in their approach to this problem can take some satisfaction from the fact that the demand factor at work in the Canadian economy today is so strong, and that it is a reflection of the forces of recovery at work in the economy. This fact was completely glossed over yesterday by hon. members opposite and was cheerfully ignored by them while they chose to dwell upon the more unfavourable factors of any situation that they found available for their purpose.
The total of bank loans has a further interest for this house. As hon. members are aware we, as a government, have urged the banks to lend, and lend substantially, under the provisions of the National Housing Act in order to assist in home construction, and in that way to spur employment in this country. Well, the chartered banks have responded, and I wish to indicate the way in which the needs of our housing program have also created demands upon the available cash resources of the banks. Here I give the figures of insured residential mortgages held by the banks. I begin with June, 1957 as a significant date, and the house will note a steady rise in investment by the chartered banks of Canada in insured residential mortgages under the National Housing Act.
When we came to office in June, 1957 the chartered banks were holding a total of $501 million of these mortgages. By January, 1958 that figure had risen to $591 million; by January, 1959 to $791 million; by March 25, 1959 to $823 million, and by April 15, the last date for which figures are available, to $828 million. Here again is a factor in demand which I think will give satisfaction to the house and to the country.
I have spoken about the forces of demand at work in the money market today. Let me turn now to the forces affecting supply. I am sure I do not need to remind the house

Monetary Policy
that Canada is a country which chronically suffers from a shortage of capital. It is a young country with tremendous resources to be developed. It needs capital for the development of those resources. Canada is the largest net importer of capital in the world, not just on a per capita basis but on a national, an absolute, basis. There is an impression in some parts of the world that because Canada has a high standard of living, Canada must have available a substantia] volume or surplus of capital. That is not so. I had frequent occasion in the talks I had with governments in Asia last autumn to point out that fact. Canada is the largest importer of capital in the world.
What are the sources of capital? In the first place, savings are an important source of capital, the savings of persons and the savings of corporations. The other source, so far as Canada is concerned, is the capital imported from foreign sources. We need to give encouragement to individuals and corporations to practise the virtue of saving in order to create capital so they may rely on themselves and in that way help to sustain the growth of the economy. And when socialist members of this house seek to crush the corporations in this country, they should bear in mind that corporations are themselves a source of capital, and that if the corporations are to be crushed there will be so much less capital available for the expansion of the economy and the creation of more jobs for Canadians.
As far as foreign sources of capital are concerned, we may wish as Canadians that we had available from domestic sources all the capital we need and that we did not stand in need of foreign capital. However, we are not in that happy situation. We do need this foreign capital; and therefore we must-and this is the policy of this government-create a climate hospitable to foreign capital investment.
What has been the course of the movement of capital into Canada? In 1956 the total of capital movement into Canada measured by the balance of international payments was $1,372 million. In 1957 it was $1,366 million. In 1958, notwithstanding the economic situation we experienced, especially in the earlier part of the year, foreign capital came into Canada to the extent of $1,112 million. And while one cannot prophesy with any certainty what may be the amount of foreign capital coming into this country in this year of 1959, it is quite evident from the figures I have given that there is no substantial reduction in the volume of such capital entering Canada. Therefore we may look with reasonable confidence for the continuation

of a substantial volume of foreign capital coming into Canada for investment.
We shall, of course, have to bear in mind what effect this will have on exchange rates. The Canadian dollar has been at a premium since 1952. To some Canadians this is a matter of pride. It is a matter of economic advantage to people who have to meet obligations in terms of United States dollars. It helps some Canadians, and it works to the disadvantage of others. When the Canadian dollar is at a premium in relation to the United States dollar, the import of foreign goods into Canada is facilitated. An obstacle, to the extent of the premium, is placed in the way of exports of Canadian goods to other countries. Similarly, in relation to the movement of capital, the inward movement of United States capital into Canada has the effect of boosting the premium on the United States dollar, and this is what we have to bear in mind. The outward movement of capital from Canada to the United States, or the return of capital to that country, would of course have the effect of reducing the premium on the Canadian dollar in relation to the United States dollar. We need United States capital on proper terms, and the premium is the price that is being paid at the present time. One regrets the fact that it works to the disadvantage of exporters. This is not a matter of government choice at all; this is a matter of the operation of the free forces in a free economy.
Let me now address myself directly to the question of supply within Canada to meet the extraordinarily heavy demand at the present time. Last night I spoke of the components of money supply in Canada. I pointed out that they consist of currency in circulation and deposits in the chartered banks. We are told by hon. gentlemen opposite that there is something heinous about the increase in the money supply that occurred in the year 1958. Certainly and admittedly a substantial increase occurred in the money supply in Canada in that year.
At the end of 1958 the money supply was $13,247 million and at the end of 1957 it was $11,923 million. The increase in money supply in 1958 in Canada was $1,324 million. But, Mr. Speaker, there was a very good reason for that increase in money supply in Canada last year. I say to you that if the money supply had not increased in Canada in 1958 the first persons to be critical of the fact that it had not increased would have been hon. gentlemen opposite, the members of the official opposition.
The fact is that the amount of currency was increased last year and the chartered bank deposits of Canadians increased last

year. Apparently that is a matter of regret to hon. gentlemen in the official opposition. These increased, however, not because the government decreed any increase in currency or in money supply. The Bank of Canada, as I pointed out last night, has the authority and is the only body in Canada that has the authority to determine the volume of currency issued. What the government did in the parallel field of fiscal action was to take steps with a view to imparting vigour to the Canadian economy. We deliberately budgeted for a deficit last year with a view to giving impetus and strength to the forces of recovery at work in the economy.
Let us look at what has happened since October 1 of last year. Hon. gentlemen in the official opposition who have something critical to say about the increased money supply should have been saying it in 1958 when such criticisms would have had some relevancy to the conditions then existing; but oh, no, these Rip van Winkles wake up in 1959 and discover a situation existed in 1958 which, if you please, ceased to exist on October 1, 1958.
How are you enjoying your slumber at this moment?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The situation has been substantially different since. Indeed, the money supply in Canada has contracted since then. I give you just the figures from December to April 15. The figure for the money supply in Canada on April 15 was $13,205 million. There was an actual drop of $42 million in that 3|-month period.

Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the minister would permit a question. Would the minister care to tell us what kind of capital was the increase in the money supply of last year in the amount of something over $1 billion to which he referred.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is money supply. The hon. gentleman will have to distinguish as best he can between capital and money supply. This is money supply measured in terms of the combined total of currency in circulation and deposits in the chartered banks. What hon. members in the opposition had to say about this matter yesterday is stale. They were complaining about a condition which ceased to exist on October 1, 1958. Indeed, as I have indicated, the money supply has been dropping in recent months.
As to the future, I am not going to attempt any prophecy as to what is likely to be the trend in the volume of money supply. I do know that the Bank of Canada watches this situation very closely, and in whatever may be done in this respect I am sure the house 66968-9-198
Monetary Policy
would expect a balance to be preserved between the needs of expanding business on the one hand-the forces of recovery-and on the other hand restraints against the dangers of inflation.
There is one other possible source of supply to which I shall give just a word of comment. It is the bank reserves. The government has no control whatever over bank reserves; I wish to make that abundantly clear. It is the Bank Act of this country which in section 71 lays down the requirements imposed by parliament upon the chartered banks of Canada in relation to the maintenance of their cash reserves. Section 71, subsection 1 reads:
71. (1) The bank shall maintain a cash reserve in the form of a deposit with the Bank of Canada and of Bank of Canada notes held by the bank, and such reserve shall be not less on the average during any month than 8 per cent, or such other percentage as may be fixed by the Bank of Canada under the provisions of the Bank of Canada Act, of such of its deposit liabilities as are payable in Canadian currency.
That is the statutory obligation of the banks, to maintain a cash reserve of 8 per cent measured in terms of deposit liabilities. In addition to that figure the banks of this country have for the past three years maintained an additional reserve of 7 per cent which has been held in the form of treasury bills and day to day loans. The reserves of the banks in the period since this government came into office reached their peak in May of 1958, when the average liquid asset ratio of all the chartered banks reached 18.1 per cent. From that time, as the forces of recovery have gathered more and more momentum, that figure has been reduced and the last figure available at April 22 showed that the over-all average liquid asset ratio of bank reserves, had dropped to 15.48 per cent, a very substantial reduction since the high of May, 1958.
If hon. members opposite are going to deal fairly with this question when they criticize the situation of today they will have to tell the house what their position is in relation to money supply, the creation of an increase in money supply, and what their position is in regard to bank reserves. They have not said a word about those subjects, and I think we well know why. If the 7 per cent reserve that the banks hold in terms of treasury bills and day to day loans were reduced it would result in a liquidation of treasury bills and more pressure on the treasury bill rate in this country. But hon. members opposite did not have the frankness to face up to that fact yesterday or even to acknowledge it. I do not think, Mr. Speaker, that anyone in this house is going to propose that the Bank Act of this country should be

Monetary Policy
amended to reduce the requirement under section 71 that the banks should hold an 8 per cent reserve in cash.
I should like to turn now to what I think is a very interesting commentary upon the kind of speeches we listened to yesterday from hon. members of the opposition. They gloried in the increase in interest rates, and they gloried also in whatever signs of weakness they could find in the bond market. They would have left the impression, had they been able to do so, that this is a new phenomenon and that it has not occurred before. Well, Mr. Speaker, I know the house is not going to be misled by that type of erring propaganda on the part of the opposition, but let me place on the record some interesting figures illustrating the way bond prices went in the days of the Liberal government.
I am going to compare two dates, March 29, 1955, with June 21, 1957, when that Liberal government went out of office, and I am going to give the house seven or eight outstanding Canadian bond issues so the house can see what happened to the quoted values of those Canada bonds in the market between those two dates. Three per cents, due May 1, 1958, dropped from 103.35 to 98.90, a loss of 4.45; 3 per cents, due October 1, 1963, dropped from 102.45 to 90.625, a drop of 11.825; 3 per cents, due September 1, 1966, dropped from 102.50 to 88.375, a drop of 14.125; 2| per cents due June 15, 1968, dropped from 99.50 to 84.75, a drop of 14.75; 3J per cents, due June 1, 1976, dropped from 102.125 to 87.25, a drop of 14.875; 3| per cents, due June 15, 1978, dropped from 108.50 to 94.50, a drop of 14; 3i per cents, due October 1, 1979, dropped from 102.125 to 86.875, a drop of 15.25; and the 3 per cent perpetuals dropped from 96.625 to 79.75, a drop of 16.875.
All these drops Mr. Speaker, occurred before we ever came into office, and you will see, therefore, how hollow in the mouths of hon. members opposite rings the cry about the weakness of the bond market and the rise in interest rates, and the talk about the loss of confidence in government of Canada issues. I will tell you, Mr. Speaker; if there was loss of confidence it occurred in that period from 1955 to 1957, infinitely more significantly than in any period since.
Will the minister permit a question? Will he tell us whether during that period the government was a net borrower in the market?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with respect to the entire period I am not prepared to make a quick answer to that question. There were periods when the government

was a net borrower; there were periods when the position was reversed.
The figures I have given, Mr. Speaker, were for government of Canada bonds, but I think it is worth reflecting also upon what happened to the values in the market of outstanding provincial issues in this period of Liberal rule. Again I have the figures for the two dates, March 29, 1955 and June 21, 1957. Alberta, 2| per cents, due March 1, 1970 dropped from 98.50 to 84.50, a drop of 14; British Columbia 3 per cents, due December 15, 1969 dropped from 98.25 to 83, a drop of 15.25; Manitoba 4| per cents, due October 1, 1968 dropped from 107 to 93.25, a drop of 13.75; New Brunswick 4-J per cents, due February 2, 1965 dropped from 106 to 95, a drop of 11 points; Nova Scotia 3J per cents, due November 15, 1970 dropped from 99 to 84, a drop of 15 points; Ontario 4 per cents due June 30, 1972 dropped from 106.75 to 91.25, a drop of 15.50; Quebec 3 per cents, due July 1, 1969 dropped from 97.25 to 84.75, a drop of 12.50; Saskatchewan 3,1 per cents, due April 15, 1972 dropped from 97.75 to 81.75, a drop of 16 points.
In the face of that unhappy record, Mr. Speaker, hon. members of the opposition undertake to say any evidence of weakness in the bond market today, or any evidence of increase in interest rates, in the face of the extraordinary demand for commercial credit today, is the responsibility of the present government, and that the people have lost confidence in government of Canada credit because of some failure on the part of the present government. Let them clean their own house before they undertake to level empty, baseless charges of that kind against others.
I have drawn attention to the fact that the field of monetary action belongs to the Bank of Canada; the field of fiscal action belongs to the government. I emphasize, Mr. Speaker, that the increase in money supply in 1958 was accompanied by deficit financing, deliberate deficit financing on the part of the government, all done with a view to stimulating the forces of recovery in the economy. Today recovery is clearly under way, and the policy in regard to money supply was moderated as from the first day of October so as to permit recovery to proceed but without inflation. Similarly, in the present budget fiscal policy was modified by the government with the same object in view, to avoid inflation while at the same time putting no obstacle in the way of the recovery movement in the Canadian economy.
This requires the best judgment that the Bank of Canada on the one hand and the government on the other can muster; but,

Mr. Speaker, let hon. members be fair about it and recognize where responsibility rests and the extent to which the conditions that exist today are attributable to the steps taken to stimulate recovery in Canada. They do not want recovery; that seems to be the net effect of their observations here today.
Yesterday.

As I pointed out in the budget speech, Mr. Speaker-

As I pointed out, with a good response to our Canada savings bond campaign next

autumn our own market borrowings in 195960, should be less than one-half of the $1,220 million which we borrowed in the market in the fiscal year 1958-59.
There is one other subject, to which I am obliged by the amendment to turn; not that I enjoy making a speech of such length as this, far from it. However, hon. members opposite in their amendment sought to embrace every possible subject that in their ingenuity they could think up for the occasion. If I may use common language, they have taken in the whole waterfront in this amendment and they have obliged me to speak on these subjects at some length.
Amongst the many matters of which they complain in this extraordinary fake amendment of theirs is the conversion loan. It is significant, I think, that they have not chosen to condemn the conversion loan. What they have talked about instead has been one aspect of it, or two at the most. They talked about "the errors and inequities" associated with the conversion loan. I would have thought that if hon. members opposite had any pretence to fortitude they would have come out and said they did not like the conversion loan and invited the house to condemn the conversion loan. However, courage failed them at that point; courage fled, and what they resorted to was a reference to what they called the "errors and inequities" associated with the conversion loan. There were no errors or inequities associated with the conversion loan.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Just blunders.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) had been here yesterday perhaps he would have supplied what was lacking in this amendment. He would have had the courage to come out and condemn the conversion loan in this amendment instead of taking part in this hide and seek game that his colleagues played yesterday with this subject.
I am obliged to say something about this conversion loan. This subject was discussed quite a few times in this house during the last session, and on one or two occasions in this session, but if hon. members opposite insist upon a further discussion then I am happy to accommodate them. I shall make some general comments, Mr. Speaker, about the features of the loan and the conditions associated with it before I come down to deal with some of the statements that were uttered here yesterday.
The conversion loan of 1958 was the greatest financial operation in Canada's history. It was a very great success, and indeed far exceeded our expectations. I should like to remind the house of the conditions in the

Monetary Policy
summer of 1958 under which this enterprise was undertaken. In April, 1958 the rising trend in bond prices was arrested and indications of economic recovery appeared, with their prospective concomitant of a growing demand for money from non-government sources. In the United States worry about the size of the government's deficit and borrowing requirements and fears of inflation emerged at an early stage, and a sharp and continuing decline in bond prices set in. The last reduction in the discount rate of federal reserve banks of the United States was made on April 18. Bond prices in that country hit their peak on April 21. A decline then set in which was temporarily interrupted in the latter half of May, but then continued with little interruption until October. A further decline of bond prices began in the last week of November, and hon. members are familiar with what has happened since that time.
It was not to be expected that Canadian bond prices would always follow United States bond prices, even in direction over short intervals, let alone in degree of movement. But undoubtedly developments in the United States are bound, soon or later, to have a weighty influence on developments in Canada; and so it was in 1958. The average maturity of public debt had been shortening for several years, both in the United States and Canada. The large volume of securities falling due for repayment each year was a matter of concern to fiscal authorities in both countries and a serious handicap to the sale of new issues for cash in a period of government deficits. By the end of June the market atmosphere was very unfavourable to new financing.
While the government of Canada needed large sums of new money in the immediate future funds could be obtained as a last resort from the banks, with the Bank of Canada providing increased cash reserves to the chartered banks, but after the large scale purchase of government securities by the banks and corresponding monetary expansion in the preceding 12 months this would have been regarded as dangerously inflationary, unless other steps could be taken simultaneously to deal with the public debt structure and make possible the sale of future issues of government bonds to non-bank investors. At the same time some way had to be found to reduce the heavy proportion of short term bonds and increase substantially the proportion of long term bonds.
The five victory loans totalling $6,416 million had ultimate maturity dates between January 1, 1959 and September 1, 1966. In addition, all these issues were callable on or before September 1, 1961. This prospect, in

addition to the non-victory loan maturities and the need for heavy new borrowings, made debt reorganization imperative if a high degree of confusion and demoralization of the bond market was to be avoided, and a sound basis created for financing Canada's expansion and development.
Conversion of all five victory loan issues was more equitable, more efficient and less costly than a piecemeal approach could possibly have been. Fundamental to the project was the idea that it would be easier to sell the public long term bonds in exchange for bonds which they already held than to sell them long term bonds for cash. The prospects of cash requirements of the Canadian government for several years ahead were also a major consideration. It was urgently important to improve the government's debt structure, to reduce the overhang of refinancing which would have to be done in addition to new money financing and to put as much of the government's debt as possible on a long term basis.
The terms of the conversion loan were developed on the best advice having regard to the objective, the erosion which had occurred in the market and the measures necessary to attract public investment in the long term sector. The conversion loan was an overwhelming success. A total of more than $5,803 million, or more than 90 per cent of the outstanding victory bonds, was converted.
The interest rates set on the new conversion loan bonds reflected market yields prevailing at the time while taking into account the size of the operation. Exaggerated and distorted statements have been made as to the burden which these higher conversion loan interest rates will impose. Such statements, and we have heard many of them in the house, all of them mistaken and misleading, erroneously assume that each victory loan issue could have been refunded at maturity at a 3 per cent interest rate. The evidence is all to the contrary, especially having regard to the fact that the overhang on the market would still have persisted. Rates at the time of such refundings would almost certainly have been higher than is now the case.
The coupon rate on all of the victory loans was 3 per cent. The average coupon rate on all of the bonds converted is now 4 per cent. Since 61 per cent of the conversion went into the 14-year and 25-year maturities and since, having regard to call dates, all of the victory loans were of three years or less maturity, this is a very satisfactory average coupon rate. The interest payable on the $6,416 million of bonds before conversion was $192,480,000. It is now $250,705,000, an increase of $58,225,000 or about 30 per cent.

The conversion loan was a constructive and stabilizing factor in the market, particularly in the long term sector. The benefits of its influence accrue to provincial and municipal borrowers who would otherwise have had to face a high rate structure inevitably resulting from the uncertainty and imminence of these huge maturities overhanging the market.
I have said that the conversion operation was an overwhelming success. It has earned the outspoken admiration of the governments of other countries. This success was achieved with the full co-operation of the Bank of Canada. Before conversion only 17 per cent of the government of Canada's debt, other than savings bonds, was in maturities over ten years. After the conversion fully 43 per cent was in such maturities. Before conversion 39 per cent of the debt, other than savings bonds, was in market issues with maturities of less than two years. After the conversion 25 per cent was in such issues. The average maturity of the public debt, other than savings bonds, was lengthened from 6i years to 10J years in Canada and became double the comparable average maturity in the United States.
While prices of government bonds have declined in recent months, the benefits of the conversion loan operation continue. I should like to add a comment on the market price quotations of these new conversion bonds. I think it is fair that in making this comparison we compare the rates prevailing in the market prior to the time the conversion loan operation was launched with those prevailing in the market on these issues in the autumn following.
The government at no time said that it would support current market prices on the conversion loan. While the Bank of Canada, acting as the government's fiscal agent, normally operates in a manner to stabilize the after-market for a short period for each new loan, it is not the government's policy to support the bond market over longer periods.
The government's obligation is to pay a fixed rate of interest on the conversion loan bonds and redeem them in full at maturity. Far from having given any indication of supporting the market price of the conversion loan, the government expressly disclaimed any such undertaking in the House of Commons.
I point, Mr. Speaker, in this connection to the question asked in the house by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) last September and my answer to his question. It is the play of the forces in the market which determines the day to day price of bonds. It happens that largely as a result of the continued erosion of the United States bond market there were weakening effects on market offerings for government issues in Canada evident in the
