themselves because the high interest rate would make them more financially secure. This conversion loan would also be a help to the provinces and municipalities in their borrowings. We might read into the record an item that appeared in the Montreal Gazette of July 15, 1958 which was entitled, "Sound Money Policy-The Prime Minister". It reads:
Prime Minister Diefenbaker tonight urged victory bond holders to participate in the huge bond conversion campaign with the same spirit and determination that brought distinction to Canada in the second world war.
He emphasized, in speaking over the largest radio and television network ever set up in Canada, that there was no element of compulsion in the bond-swap plan.
Holders of victory loan bonds didn't have to trade for the new, higher-yield conversion bonds if they didn't want to.
But he argued that the conversion of some $6,400 million in victory bonds, together with other federal operations being planned and undertaken, "will make it possible for our nation to embark on a new era of peacetime prosperity far and beyond anything we have ever known".
The conversion was "in every sense antiinflationary," he added as he and Finance Minister Fleming joined forces to explain the conversion plan to the public. It was in line with a "sound money" policy, not involving any new borrowings by the government.
Later in the article, we find this:
Mr. Fleming said the conversion loan will "simplify our debt structure" and make for more orderly debt management, easing the way to financing of future developments without creating inflation.
This great mass of $6,500 million of short term bonds (the victory bonds) overhanging the bond market has produced a feeling of uncertainty in the minds of both borrowers and lenders.
This uncertainty has made borrowing more difficult and more costly to the provinces and municipalities and to other borrowers. I am sure that when we have successfully refunded this great mass of bonds and spread them out over a much longer period of time, a healthier tone and much greater confidence will develop in the bond market.
This will benefit not only the dominion government but also the provinces, the municipalities and directly or indirectly all other classes of borrowers as well.
According to the minister this conversion loan has proven to be a colossal success. I am not an expert in these financial matters nor are the 17 million Canadian people. It seems to me that the real test of whether or not this conversion loan was a success is to examine whether or not the government achieved the objective it had in mind when the conversion loan campaign was launched. Have we actually embarked on a new era of prosperity, the like of which we have never seen in the country? Are higher interest rates the new Conservative barometer which indicates a new prosperity we are having? Have increased interest rates made it more

easy for the municipalities and provinces to be able to extricate themselves from the financial plight in which they are now placed?
It is evident now that the conversion loan was not a well thought out plan which the government had conceived in order to stabilize our economy and in order to stop inflation. It was no such thing. It was another political expedient and the government embarked on this method in order to face the great deficits that it foresaw not only for this year but for several years to come. Whether or not the government admits it, up to now the conversion loan has been a failure because it has not achieved the objectives which the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance set forth with respect to the loan. The very fact that the bank rate increased after the anti-inflationary budget, as some people call it, was brought down a short time ago is complete indication that we have very little hope that the conversion loan will be a success in the future.
In his statement on television as part of his effort to sell the conversion loan the Prime Minister stated that the conversion loan was in every sense anti-inflationary. As a matter of fact, even for an amateur it was quite difficult to understand how the conversion loan would be anti-inflationary because in order to sell the bonds the government decided to pay an interest rate the like of which had never been paid before. Of course, if federal government bonds were bearing high interest rates all other bonds would indeed have to carry higher interest rates. To my mind that has started the ball of inflation rolling with even greater rapidity than before.
But there is another thing which I believe was inflationary and it is something which I think we might well stop to consider. The government fixed an artificial price on the bonds and bonds that were worth $94 on the market were being sold for $100. Those people who are greatly experienced in the matter of bonds, who have been dealing with bonds all their lives, indeed foresaw a wonderful opportunity whereby they would sell their bonds for $100, a price they had never hoped to get, and reinvest their gain in shorter term bonds. As a matter of fact, $371 million was "disinvested" in this way.
But the great majority of people who held bonds, the people to whom the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance appealed on television, the people to whom the Prime Minister gave assurances that Canadian bonds including victory bonds had the strength of the rock of Gibraltar, were a little dismayed, because of their inexperience in dealing with bonds, to see that the value of their bonds
Monetary Policy
kept declining. As a result, they sold their bonds for $92.50, having lost confidence in the government and in the victory loan bonds.
I am beginning to wonder whether there is not something absolutely immoral and economically unsound about fixing an artificial price for a bond which has no relation to its real market value.
In order to facilitate the flotation of the conversion loan the government also expanded its money supply so that the conversion loan, which was supposed to be antiinflationary, was accompanied by an alarming increase in the money supply. In my opinion, . since the Conservatives have had the responsibility of office the government has created every penny it has borrowed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What nonsense!

This, of course, is no different from the straight printing of currency. For the more than 20 months from the end of July, 1957 to April 1, 1959 the entire increase in the government debt, including savings bonds, has been paralleled by an increase in the money supply. During that period the gross debt increased by $1,764 million and the money supply was increased by $1,795 million. Moreover, the increase in the marketable debt, that is, gross debt less savings bonds, has been $1,187 million which corresponds to an increase of $1,217 million in the holdings of the Bank of Canada and the commercial banks. This means that the Conservative government has in fact decided to monetize its deficit.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Will the hon. member tell me how the government can operate in the field of monetary policy?
As a matter of fact, it has acted in the field of monetary policy-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The government?
-and what I have just said is in fact the result of the government's administration in this field.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The minister does not understand. He is hard of hearing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member for Laurier does not understand the difference between fiscal and monetary policy or the difference between the government and the Bank of Canada and their respective responsibilities.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I can explain it to you very quickly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You were not here last night.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
No, but I have listened to a lot of guff from you this afternoon.

Monetary Policy

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Is it over your head?

As I say, I think it is clear that the Conservative government has in fact decided to monetize its deficit. I admit that I had to look into the matter of monetization and in my research I came across an article in the Commercial and Financial Chronicle of April 23 by the secretary of the treasury of the United States, Robert B. Anderson, and this is what he says:
The fact that fiscal matters are little understood, even by some rather prominent and otherwise well informed people, was brought home to me one day when a visitor in my office remarked: "You talk of the dangers of monetization of the debt, Mr. Secretary. You know I just don't believe there is such a danger, probably because I don't quite understand what monetization means."
The Hon. Robert Anderson gave this explanation:
I said this to my visitor: "Now suppose I wanted to write cheques of $100 million starting tomorrow morning but the treasury was out of money. If I called up a bank and said, 'will you loan me $100 million at Si per cent for six months if I send you over a note to that effect,' the banker would probably say, 'yes, I will.'
Where would he get the $100 million with which to credit the account of the United States treasury? Would he take it from the account of someone else? No, certainly not. He would merely create that much money, subject to reserve requirements, by crediting our account in that sum and accepting the government's note as an asset. When I had finished writing cheques for $100 million the operation would have added that sum to the money supply. Now certainly that approaches the same degree of monetization as if I had called down to the bureau of engraving and printing and said: 'Please print me up $100 million worth of greenbacks which I can pay out tomorrow.' ''
That is exactly what the government has done. The government has paralleled the increase in our national debt by an equal increase in our money supply, and to my mind that is a classic definition of inflation.
Then, of course, it is also quite difficult to understand how, according to the Minister of Finance, the highest bank rates in Canada's history can be helpful to the provinces and the municipalities. We recall all the speeches that were made by members of the government and all the crocodile tears that were shed about the financial plight of the provinces and the municipalities and the fact that they were so greatly in debt it was very difficult for them to get out. We also remember the promises that were made that the provinces and the municipalities would have a greater share of the tax dollar and that borrowings would be made far more easy. It seems to me that the increase in the bank rate and the increase in rates generally will make it virtually impossible for

the provinces and municipalities to extricate themselves from the financial plight they are in.
As a matter of fact, this particular increase can only ensure the provinces and the municipalities that they are going to stay with their debt. Promises made were to the effect, "We will allow you a greater share of the tax dollar; We will facilitate your borrowing powers," but as a matter of fact the action of the government means that the federal government will collect the tax and the municipalities and the provinces will have to borrow at higher interest rates.
I would like to quote also from the Montreal Gazette, an article which I think is quite accurate and which reflects very much my own way of thinking. It is an article by Mr. John Meyer in the Gazette for July 16, 1958:
The federal government is exchanging one set of fixed charges, the interest it must pay on victory bonds outstanding, for another, higher, set.
At the same time, it has established a higher base cost for credit. All other borrowing must now conform to these new rates at a subsequent higher cost to the borrowers.
The next paragraph is entitled, "Tough on Taxpayers":
The higher cost of borrowing, in so far as governments are concerned, means an increase in the fixed charges which taxpayers must meet. It means that more of the tax revenue must now be committed to payment of interest rates, leaving less for other purposes.
The higher cost of borrowing means too that the possibilities of tax reduction are that much more limited.
As a matter of fact, we really know now that that turned out to be very true. I continue:
It means further that the proceeds of borrowing by corporations are reduced by the higher interest rates they must pay. Some corporations will be forced, undoubtedly, to postpone their borrowing or, alternatively, increase the amount: neither is desirable.
Finally, it will mean an increased American demand for Canadian dollars as junior governments and corporations try to reduce their borrowing costs by borrowing at the lower interest rates prevailing in the United States.
And that demand for Canadian funds will push an already high premium higher still, to the further disadvantage of Canadian producers for export and domestic consumption alike.
Does this sound, as though we were entering into a new era of prosperity, the like of which we have never seen before? Does this sound as though we were entering upon a sound monetary policy? The conversion loan and all that goes with it was supposed to be anti-inflationary in every respect. I do not believe that anyone can come to the conclusion that the Prime Minister did, and as

the Minister of Finance has today when he claims his conversion loan was indeed a complete success.
Before finishing there is something I would like to read into the record which I believe is important at this time. It is an extract from a television broadcast that was made on April 21, 1959. I believe this transcription to be correct. It was taken from the sound track directly. However, if it is not correct I am quite sure that the Minister of Finance will correct me, and I wish to be fair about this.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member who took it? Did my hon. friend take it?
No, I did not take it, but it was taken from the sound track.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Who did take it?

I could not tell my hon. friend who took it, but it was taken by a machine and transcribed by one of the stenographers. However, if the hon. minister feels it is not correct then I shall be happy to have his correction. During the conversation questions were asked of the minister. One of these questions, asked by Mr. Blakely, was:
But governments can also contribute to high costs. I know that the Conservatives argued this most forcefully for about 22 years. They used to say, what's wrong with this Liberal government? They say that if you spend your own money it is inflationary, but if they take it from you and spend it for you, why then, it is non-inflationary. What nonsense this is. Are you not doing the same thing here?
Then the Minister of Finance:
No, no, no, no. You are quoting the things that we said in the days in opposition, when the government of that day was making a virtue of taking money from people, not to meet the exigencies of balancing the budget or even coming close to it or in view to reducing a deficit. But they were taking money far more than what was needed to meet the ordinary expenses of government on the theory that they could do a better job of managing the expenditure and handling of the people's money than they could do themselves, and we never have been of that opinion and I hope we never will.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, I could make the very obvious observation that it must take an incredible amount of gall, sanctimony and cockiness for the Minister of Finance to make such a self-accusing and boomerang statement so soon after the "We knew it all" budget that he brought down just a few weeks ago. But if this statement means anything at all it means that the government does not intend to budget for a surplus in order to reduce the national debt, and that the government proposes to continue to balance the increase in the national debt by an increase in the
Monetary Policy
money supply. As I said before, I think that is absolutely inflationary and detrimental to the Canadian economy.
The last thing I should like to mention, is this. In his remarks the minister asked that the Liberal opposition should make some constructive suggestions. We feel a little as though it would be almost impertinent on the part of the Liberal opposition to make any suggestion to the Conservative government who, in 1957, had, according to them, all the answers and all the solutions.
Give them the chance and they will hang themselves.

I would say, that I am a little surprised now to hear, after 20 months in office, the Minister of Finance calling on the Liberals for help in order to get himself out of the predicament he has put himself into. But if we were to make suggestions from this side of the house, then we would have to start right from the beginning. First of all, the Liberals would not have made the extravagant promises which the Conservatives made, and not having made the promises we would not have such a great debt. Not having the great debt we would not have had to borrow so much. Not having had to borrow so much we would not have had to raise the interest rate so high. Not having had to raise the interest rate so high we would not have had to have such an increase in the supply of money. Not having had to have such an increase in the supply of money, we would not have had as much inflation. Not having as much inflation we could go back to the very useful method of budgeting for a surplus when there was the danger of inflation, and bugeting for a deficit when there was a danger of recession.
I will admit that this method, which proved to be so successful in the past, is not as spectacular or as fancy as the Conservative's great conversion loan, but it certainly had one distinct advantage-it worked.

In his
long introductory remarks last evening and in his two-hour marathon speech this afternoon, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) has insisted that the government has no influence on the rate established by the Bank of Canada for the chartered banks. And then he told us that interest rates have now returned to those of the summer of 1957, but he was very careful to add that the government has no jurisdiction over them. He next accused members of the opposition of flaring up when interest rates are rising, and of saying nothing when interest rates were going down. We know where the Minister of Finance was when the

Monetary Policy
rates were going down, and we know where he is when the rates are going up. In fact, when the rates were going down the minister, both inside and outside this house, took credit, or gave credit to the government, for the decline in the rates, and I should like to remind him at this time of the reply he gave in this chamber a little over a year ago on January 31, 1958, as reported on page 4089 of Hansard, when he was asked a question by the then hon. member for Nanaimo.

May I address a supplementary question to the Minister of Finance? Can he inform the house if this change from a tight money position has been the result of some action by the government, and what the action has been?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, there has been action on the part of the government. I do not say that the reduction is attributable entirely to the government's action, but it certainly is in line with government policy, and is in part attributable to it. The fact is that we have been seeking to bring about, with the means open to us, a reduction in this rate. I am not at liberty, and it has never been the practice, to indicate to the house all the government operations or the operations of the fiscal agent of the government in these matters, but I can assure my hon. friend that this reduction, which I am happy to report this morning, is fully in line with government policy.
Those were the words of the Minister of Finance when interest rates were going down.
But that was before the election.

Yes, fortunately for them it was before the election. But what is the minister's new doctrine in this respect? The doctrine which he expressed last evening was that the government is responsible for fiscal policy and that the Bank of Canada is responsible for monetary policy, including the bank rate. This is a complete vindication of what Mr. Harris was saying when he was minister of finance. It is, in fact, exactly what he used to say. What a change has come about in the attitude taken by the minister. He contends that our amendment seeks to hold the government responsible for all that has happened in the field of monetary action. That is not so. We certainly did not do this in our amendment, and I will come to that later on. But that is certainly what the minister was doing when he was sitting on this side of the house as the hon. member for Eglinton. Does this mean that the minister, then, had not read the statute law enacted by this parliament, as he accused some of the members on this side of the house of not doing when he spoke last evening and this afternoon? It certainly would appear so if we are to judge the

minister by the statements he made when he was sitting on the opposition side.
I am sure that no one who followed the remarks made by the minister could fail to realize that the hon. gentleman has completely missed the nature of our indictment. He is trying to avoid his responsibilities and trying to blame the Bank of Canada for what is happening today in the field of debt management and monetary policy. It is typical of the attitude of the present government to lay all their troubles on the shoulders of someone else, if not on the shoulders of the previous administration, then on those of the Bank of Canada. What does our indictment really seek to do? We blame the government for the mistakes and inequities associated with the conversion loan, which was a failure notwithstanding the statement made this afternoon by the minister himself. We blame the government for the error it made when it offered to buy victory bonds at par, thereby inducing well-informed people not to convert. We blame the government for including the seventh, eighth and ninth victory issues in the operation, thereby giving a scope to the procedure which was quite unnecessary and ill-timed in the light of the depressed condition of the market.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question? Are we to infer from his remarks that he approves of the conversion loan as applied to the fifth and sixth victory loans?
If there was a necessity to convert those loans, the hon. gentleman was in a better position to obtain this information than any member on the opposition side.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Would the hon. member answer my question?

Monetary Policy
exert our efforts in the international field towards achieving conditions of durable economic growth and monetary stability throughout the world.
Here we had a warning from the governor of the Bank of Canada to the effect that the threat of inflation was far from being checked as the minister claimed it was on November 14 of 1957.
Let me place on the record a further statement made by the minister in November 1957. This has to do directly with the bank rate situation. Again, at page 1162 of Hansard of November 14, 1957, we find a statement by the minister in these words:
In this house two days ago I referred to the fact that in the past two months interest rates paid by this country on its treasury bills had dropped by 3/10 of 1 per cent. I am happy to report that in the weekly issue of treasury bills today we have achieved a further reduction which now brings the reduction in the last two months to 4/10 of 1 per cent.
It was the minister who claimed "We have achieved a further reduction" on that occasion but today when the rates are going up he tells us that the government has no responsibility and that it is the responsibility of the Bank of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Would the hon.
member distinguish between treasury bill rates and Bank of Canada rates?
Yes, Mr. Speaker. May I point out that the distinction has been made two or three times in the course of this debate-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You have missed it.

-by hon. members who have spoken and it was made by the minister himself in his lengthy marathon speech.
The minister clearly stated and I repeat again:
I am happy to report that in the weekly issue of treasury bills today we have achieved a further reduction-
When things are going well the minister is prepared to take full credit but when the rates go up-and this was especially true when the Liberals were in power-the minister blames someone else. He used to say the Liberal government was responsible when the rates went up during the time we were in office but today when we have a Conservative government the minister tells us when the rates go up it is the responsibility of the Bank of Canada. The minister admitted this last evening when he stated as reported at page 3099 of Hansard of April 27:
The government does not exercise any sway in the field of monetary policy.
Those are the minister's own words. He went on to say:

The right to issue currency is vested exclusively in the Bank of Canada. Notwithstanding this fact this misguided amendment-
That is how the minister characterized our amendment. I continue:
-seeks to hold the government responsible for all that has happened in the field of monetary action.
How clearly he expressed his opinion when he stated further on:
I point out to you that the government oi Canada has no responsibility whatever for the establishment of the Bank of Canada rate.
Again, Mr. Speaker, no responsibility when the rates are going up but all the responsibility and credit when the rates are going down; this is another proof of the inconsistency of the Minister of Finance who is prepared to take the credit when the rates are going down but relegates the responsibility to where it belongs when the rates are going up.
It is not very long ago since we heard the Minister of Finance state in this house that the monetary policy of the present government was helping the municipalities by making it easier for them to borrow. In other words, faced with the largest expansion of the monetary system in any year since the war, with the largest increases in peacetime in the national debt, the highest public interest charges in Canada's history and the highest bank rate since the Bank of Canada was established, the Minister of Finance tells the provincial governments and the municipalities: "We will tax; we will collect, but you can borrow". He is very careful, however, not to mention that these municipalities will have to borrow under the highest interest rate in many generations; thus adding further to their heavy burden of taxation.
How different is the attitude of the Minister of Finance today compared with statements which he made previously either in this house or outside of this house! I mentioned a while ago some of the statements he made in his first year as Minister of Finance. It is true that the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) has claimed that there is a difference between statements made outside this house and those made inside the house. Other members of the present government have made the same claim. They make a difference between statements made as pre-election promises and accomplished facts when they have the responsibility of power. How can the minister account for the statement he made on February 23, 1958, when he said:
We have eased the burdens of the municipal governments by bringing about easier credit and lower interest rates.

How can he account for the statement he made at St. Paul, Quebec, and at Montmagny on September 28, 1958, exactly seven months ago when he said:
Credit is much easier: the provinces and municipalities in their financial operations will derive much benefit from this conversion operation.
It is now true that the benefits which were mentioned by the Minister of Finance have turned out today to be the highest interest rates in Canada's history.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They are not.

It was on July 14, 1958, in an announcement over the radio and TV about the Canada conversion loan that the Minister of Finance said:
Through this Canada conversion loan, the government is reaffirming its determination to follow policies that will maintain the soundness of our currency and the purchasing power of your dollar.
Mr. Speaker, on a point of order-
And again, when referring to higher interest rates, one could but recall that statement-
On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is reading his speech.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I presume the hon. member was not in the house this afternoon when the same point was raised and the Speaker ruled very clearly on the issue at that time.
There is a difference between the Minister of Finance making a technical speech and an hon. member making a speech.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The point has been raised by the hon. member that the hon. member for Gloucester is reading his speech. The hon. member for Gloucester knows that the practices do not permit the reading of his speech verbatim, and the house will rely on him not to breach such a practice.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I simply and respectfully draw to your attention the ruling which was made prior to this speech being made when the minister rose and spoke this afternoon, attention, attention.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I was not aware that such a ruling had been made. The ruling of the house is that in introducing technical and difficult matters, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson), or other persons making principal speeches, are allowed to follow their text more closely than other members are expected
Monetary Policy
to do. I have not heard the hon. member for Gloucester. He can tell us what he is doing and then we shall proceed.

I have substantial notes, Mr. Speaker, and I have been reading some quotations from press reports and radio and television talks by the minister himself, and these had to be quoted verbatim. I have given the reference, the dates and the places where the remarks and the statements have been made.

Which the minister did
not do.

Again I want to refer to the statement which was made about higher interest rates. One could not but recall the statement which was made in Calgary on March 14, 1958, by the Prime Minister when he claimed that:
Interest rates had fallen sharply as a result of government action since last June, from a high of 4.33 per cent to 2.89 per cent in recent weeks.
Again the Prime Minister was taking full credit for the reduction when he said the reduction had come about "as a result of government action since last June". Today the Minister of Finance and his government are dodging the responsibility when the interest rates are on the way up and are the highest in Canada's history.
Again, when speaking in Halifax on March 24, 1958, the Prime Minister in referring to finance, said, and I quote from the Halifax Chronicle-Herald, of March 25, 1958:
This government reversed the tight monetary policy of the Liberals and the interest rates have been decreased from 4.3 to 2.8 per cent.
The taxpayers today have not forgotten his federal election telecast on May 22, 1957, when the Prime Minister said:
"I think I might summarize our general view in this regard. We feel that the action taken by the government-and after all it was the government that took the action,"-raid the Prime Minister, "in restricting credit, raising interest rates and the like, has not been effective."
Following the example of his Minister of Finance, the Prime Minister himself-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. Perhaps this would be a convenient place for the hon. member to interrupt himself.

Why do you
not mark the page so you will know where to begin?

He will also know where to end.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

Monetary Policy AFTER RECESS
The house resumed at 8 p.m.
Ten.

I hear one member say
"ten". I hope, for the good of the country, we will not have to face such a situation.
The fifth point was:
5.	The highest public debt charges in Canada's history.
Is this right or wrong? If it had been wrong we would have heard the Minister of Finance interjecting "nonsense" or "it is not true". The fact that the minister did not call it nonsense shows he agrees with this statement. Oh, I know that the Minister without Portfolio for Newfoundland would say, "So what; what is the difference?" It makes a big difference to the taxpayers of this country.

What are the requirements which the Minister of Finance will have to face in the years ahead? The minister will have to again face a deficit in the year 1959-60 of over $850 million. The minister will have to provide refunding for $1,735 million before April 2, 1960. How is he going to raise the money? There are only three courses of action open to him. The first one is to increase the money supply. The second one is to increase the interest rate on government bonds, and thus make them more attractive. His third course -well, we hope he never has to take this course-would be to use force or coercion to get the money he requires. The minister did not have time to deal with this most important question in his long speech.
How is he going to get these requirements for 1959-60 which amount to well over $2.5 billion? Unfortunately, the Minister of Finance, in his swan song this afternoon, did not see fit to give us this information.
We on this side of the house are sincerely hoping that it will not be the end of the Minister of Finance. Rumours are circulating that the Prime Minister has better days ahead for the present Minister of Finance but we also realize the predicament of the Prime Minister in trying to find a successor for the present minister. I know that someone may say, "Well, maybe it could be the Minister of Justice". We all recall the statement made by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton), as reported in the Vancouver Sun of March 29, 1958:
Justice minister Fulton said Friday night the Bank of Canada will be made more responsible to parliament if the Conservatives are re-elected in the federal balloting Monday.
In view of the present policy of the government we cannot see how the minister can qualify. We have the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees). The Minister of Transport does not believe too much in budgets. After all, has he not said that very little is accomplished by budgets? We know that the government of this country needs a budget and with the Minister of Transport as minister of finance we might have to do without one.
Then there is the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) who believes in two kinds of promises, those made inside the house and those made outside the house. It would be unfortunate if the Prime Minister had such a man as minister of finance because he could not trust the promises or statements he made outside the house. Then we have the Solicitor General (Mr. Balcer), but I think it would be too much of a task for the Solicitor General because it would be imposing capital punishment on himself.
We also have the two ministers without portfolio. Maybe the Prime Minister will
Division
choose them. They could act together, be given certain responsibilities for a change and without additional cost to the treasury because they would share the task. With regard to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Hamilton), who has just taken his seat, I am afraid that his vision might be too much for the country to face because the deficits which would be the result of his vision would be almost unbelievable. As far as the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) is concerned, we might be against him taking the office because, as I said a while ago, we want a budget. The Minister of Trade and Commerce might want to keep the budget secret and we would be up against it again. The budget might be one of those hidden reports which are so hard to get and if he ever produced it we might have to go to the national Liberal federation to get copies of it.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a grievance, and I am very pleased to see the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker)

and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) in the house. This is a subject to which I have given considerable thought, and it is one which is of interest to all hon. members in this house. It concerns the question of the inadequate recompense paid to members of parliament in the present economic circumstances.
I wish to make it perfectly clear that I am making these remarks as an individual and that I have had no consultation with my party colleagues in regard to them. I feel this is a grievance which will need to be examined, and need to be examined fairly soon. This particular parliament happens to contain a higher proportion of younger men than was found in most previous parliaments and it is upon these younger men, I think, that the cost of living, and of performing the duties of a member of parliament, bears most hardly. It is true that there are a number of gentlemen who are members of parliament who do not need the extra increment which might come from a change, but the majority of members or, at least, many of them, are suffering at the present time from being involved in expenses so high that they do not allow them to carry on a proper family life and discharge their duties properly.
I know it can be said that each one of us got himself into this position and that we can get ourselves out of it. I know this is true, and I know, also, that there are many hon. members of this house who are now thinking of ways and means of getting themselves out of it without disturbing the loyalties which they have built up in their constituents. It seems to me that this is a serious question, when there are so many hon. members who are wondering how they can continue in present circumstances. It seems to me that if we want to keep the best and most active people here we will have to pay them more. And if people say to me, as no doubt some of my constituents will say to me "You are probably being overpaid now", I am willing to stand up and tell them "It is time you paid us what we are worth for the job we are doing." I hope other hon. members will say the same to their constituents.
I do not wish to go on developing this subject at the moment. If nothing is done this session, I firmly intend to put a resolution on the order paper next session asking that the government consider establishing a salary of at least $12,000 plus expense accounts paid to, at least, $3,000 a year. At any rate, that will open up the discussion. However, I hope that in view of the opinion generally held by the majority of hon. members in this house the government will give very serious consideration to the whole problem.

I cannot leave this topic without saying one word in passing about the gentlemen who report on the activities of this house and upon the doings of the members of parliament. It always seems to me that there is a tendency on their part to ridicule members of parliament and politicians in general as always looking for something extra which, perhaps, they do not deserve. I hope some of them will get down to work and do some research into the facts. Perhaps they would then find out how burdensome the situation has become for members of parliament at the present time. I think it would not be difficult to produce some actual evidence which would bear out what I have said tonight.
It is customary, when raising a grievance such as this, for anyone concerned to follow on. All hon. members have the opportunity -it is like asking a supplementary question -and if there is agreement with what I have said, I hope this opportunity will be taken to express it.

Mr. Speaker, it is not very often that I agree with the comments of a member of the C.C.F. party. Still less do I agree with the philosophy adopted, or the stand taken by the C.C.F. group in this house, but I may say that I am in complete agreement with the remarks which have just been made by the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher).
I should think offhand that many hon. members of this house if indeed not the majority of them are in agreement with the hon. member's remarks, but whether or not they will stand up and say anything at this point is another question. The possibility of any increase in our salaries or expense allowances is probably a matter for the government to decide. I am a new member of this house and perhaps I am being somewhat presumptuous in getting up and stating my views and making reference to my own circumstances. As a young man out of this house I perhaps might not be making enough money per se. Nevertheless if the press or other interested people in Canada would care to take a second look at the amount of money it costs us to come down to parliament to serve as members of this house I believe they would be quite prepared to say we should be allowed an increase whether it be in the form of an increased car allowance, or an increment in regard to expense allowances, a salary increase or whatever form it may take.
May I say only this with respect to my own position. I came out of law school only three years ago. Emerging from school I found myself in debt. Since becoming a member of parliament and coming to Ottawa to represent the people of my constituency-

speechtext:
In saying that I am not implying any kind of criticism of what was said by these hon. members at all. I am merely seeking to draw attention to the fact that the fishing industry, which I think unfortunately and regrettably in this country still has perhaps a lower average income than any other industry in Canada although it is the oldest industry in the nation, there was in part of the community where fishing is the main occupation a very regrettable failure of the fisheries last year. I am going to try in the most uncontroversial way I am capable of, to make an appeal to the government and particularly to the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker)-and I am very glad he is here this evening-on behalf of this group of citizens.
In order to found my grievance I should like briefly to refer to a question which was asked by my friend the hon. member for Trinity-Conception (Mr. Tucker) on April 14. He directed his question to the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. MacLean). I will not even read the question. It had to do with price supports. I should, however, like to read one paragraph of the minister's answer as reported at page 2659 of Hansard of April 14, in which the minister said:


I feel, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member has in mind chiefly the problem which everyone admits existed in Newfoundland last year. The fisheries prices support board held special meetings last September in Halifax and St. John's to look into the problem of the income of the Newfoundland fishermen who fish cod to be processed into dried salt cod. The advice of the fisheries prices support board was that the problem in Newfoundland was one of catch failure rather than of prices-
I believe the minister was completely right in expressing that view. If it is not contrary to the rules to say so I should like to state that although the minister and I do not agree politically I do appreciate-and I think all hon. members who are interested in the fisheries appreciate-the genuine interest that the minister has shown in the fishermen ever since he became Minister of Fisheries. I believe the minister has done everything he could be reasonably expected to do within the sphere of his department to help the fishermen and we appreciate it. I am glad to have the chance to say so. I made this comment in the committee but I am very glad to say so in this chamber if I am not transgressing the rules of the house.
This problem is one that the minister rightly pointed out in the committee. I know I should not be talking about the proceedings of the committee and I am not going to break the rules of the house by referring to it in detail. The minister pointed out that to deal with this problem was something for the cabinet and quite beyond the scope of one minister. That, of course, is quite right.
I should like to recall to the Prime Minister's mind what I am sure I do not need to do because I am sure it is very much in his mind, but I wish simply to remind him of what he said in another context in the house on August 30 of last year when he was speaking about agricultural policy. He made this statement which I am sure everyone in the house accepts in principle:
What we are trying to do is establish a concept of national policy designed to ensure equality oi opportunity for all Canadians.
Now I must say I was also encouraged to make my plea this evening by certain words used by the Prime Minister on television the other evening about the province, for part of which I am a member. I would just like to recall to hon. members' minds the words used by the Prime Minister-a very brief part of them:
There should be neither doubt nor misunderstanding about the equality of Newfoundland's status in the Canadian partnership. That equality exists as a right of our newest province's membership in the Canadian confederation. It is the earnest hope of my government that the differences may be settled as quickly as possible so that we may get together,-

And these are the words I especially want to draw to the attention of the house:
-and achieve together the raising of the general standard of living of the province and its people to that which we covet for all Canadians.
This is a problem about which I wrote to the Prime Minister a suggestion last October. I am not going to enter into any recriminations at all but the suggestion I made at that time did not commend itself to the government and it is now no longer possible for them to do anything about it. As a result of the fact that at least half the fishermen on the northeast coast of Newfoundland did not qualify for unemployment insurance because of the failure of the fisheries most of them have been driven on to relief. Most of those who did not qualify, and even some of those who did qualify for the minimum benefits, have been driven on to relief-that is at a lower scale-during this winter and many of them because of the stormy season and the other difficulties found themselves at the end of the season with cod traps that were in a bad state of repair, or cod traps that were lost entirely.
What the fishermen need if they are to be self-sufficient this year is enough money- and it would not be very much-to buy twine to fix up their traps or, in some cases where their traps are lost, enough money to get new traps so that they can go fishing and earn their own living this summer when we hope there will be a good fishery again.
Since fisheries are exclusively within the jurisdiction of the federal government, this is not a big problem in its dimensions in relation to the country as a whole. I know it applies to certain parts of Newfoundland, perhaps to most; but at any rate to the Atlantic side of Newfoundland. I believe it applies to the Magdalen islands and possibly to the Quebec-Labrador area, but there is an hon. member who represents that constituency and he can speak for himself, and perhaps to one or two limited areas in Nova Scotia. But there are those areas, and there is a problem.
It is a problem that I am sure if I put it in certain terms the Prime Minister and a good many hon. members will understand; it is the kind of problem that existed in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, particularly in Saskatchewan, in 1937, and in one or two other years, namely the problem of seed grain, when the farmers had such poor crops that many of them did not have enough grain to reseed their fields. The provincial governments lend money to the farmers and those loans were underwritten by the federal government. There, of 66968-9-199

I am not suggesting that it be a gift, or anything of that sort. It could be easily administered by the excellent officers of the Department of Fisheries who know the fishermen intimately. speakeroldname: Mr. C. R. Granger (Grand Falls-While Bay-Labrador):
subtopic: REQUEST FOR ACTION TO AID FISHERMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to add a word to what was said by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. In my own riding a great many of the fishermen are still suffering from the effects of the almost total failure of the fishery last year. This applies to Green bay, White Bay south and White Bay north, and Labrador south, particularly where very few fishermen caught enough to qualify for unemployment insurance. They caught so few fish that many of them were on relief and are still on relief. This condition is due to no fault of their own but to the failure of the fisheries. The fish simply disappeared from the coasts of Newfoundland last year. This is a poor background for a start on the new season's activities.
As has been said before, there was no special assistance to help meet what was an economic disaster to many fishermen in Newfoundland. At the present time the fishermen are beginning to outfit for the fisheries. They have to prepare their boats, replace twine, replace nets and some have to procure traps. All in all it is a considerable expense which has to be met at this time of the year if the fishermen are to be able properly to prosecute the fisheries and catch enough fish to earn a living. We hope that this year the fish will be there for them to catch.
In many instances the economic plight of the fishermen is such that they have no money and are unable to obtain credit from their merchants with which to purchase the needed materials. Unless something is done they will find themselves next fall in the same position as they were last fall. In addition to the particular plight, due to the failure of the fisheries, the fishermen of Labrador and northern Newfoundland suffered another disaster this past winter when high winds and heavy seas destroyed much fishing property; stages and fishing wharves were washed away and it is doubtful whether they can be replaced in time to prosecute the fishery unless something is forthcoming in the way of governmental help. The provincial government is sending down twine for nets and helping out to some extent in Labrador. I believe that if a proper job is to be done in helping the fishermen to reestablish themselves for this year's fishery they will need the assistance of the federal government.
I should like to say a word of tribute to the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. MacLean). I would say that all the fishermen in Newfoundland appreciate his sincere and earnest endeavours on their behalf. It is generally recognized that he has taken his job very
[Mr. Pickersgill.l

seriously and that he has at heart the interests of the fishermen, not only as important economic factors but also in the humanitarian sense.
I should like to add a word or two about those parts of the province of Newfoundland where the fisheries have been industrialized. You do not have these same recurring economic crises in those parts. It is true that this year every part of the province has been affected by the total failure of the fishery last year. However, generally speaking, wherever industrialization has taken place the fishermen are in better circumstances and find it easier to continue their operations; easier to obtain credit where necessary and generally speaking their earning power, too, is closer to that of the people in similar jobs.
I should like to mention one particular place and that is the port of St. Anthony in the northern part of Newfoundland where the fresh fish plant burned down several years ago. Ever since this great northern town has been to some extent economically depressed. At the same time St. Anthony is close to prolific fishing grounds and fishermen from isolated places are moving in to settle in St. Anthony. I would hope that the minister would take a long and careful look at the plight of this important fishing town. I would like to say a word about the moneys which have been spent by the federal and provincial governments to encourage the industrialization of the fisheries. These investments have paid dividends already and in the future they will pay richer dividends, not only in money but in human happiness.

In
view of the poor fishery last year and the lack of employment during the past winter, I strongly support the remarks of the previous speakers who have spoken on this matter. We have approximately 17,500 fishermen in Newfoundland, many of whom were unable to get unemployment insurance benefits last year because of the failure of our fishery. There was a shortage of winter work as well, and yet in spite of all this it seems that this year we will have more men prosecuting the fishery than ever before.
Now, I agree wholeheartedly with the winter works program, but because of climatic conditions in Newfoundland we did not benefit from that program to the same extent as the other provinces. Last year the federal government approved the construction of 20 community fish stages in Newfoundland at a cost of approximately $500,000. It was impossible to build these stages because of the stormy weather and heavy seas, so the program had to be abandoned. I feel that consideration should be given to doing as much of this type of work as possible during

the early summer and spring, because this would give our fishermen an opportunity to get money to assist them in buying lines, twines and ropes to repair their traps and trawls. They would get assistance in purchasing the materials required for making repairs to the boats and stages.
I feel also, Mr. Speaker, that the Department of Public Works should give serious consideration to doing some of the work on wharves and launchways in the spring rather than in the fall. If this were done, as I said previously, the men would have some money in the spring to assist them in financing their operations and thus making it unnecessary for them to depend upon the merchants to give them supplies for fishing.
I should like to add my tribute to the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. MacLean) and also to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) for their interest in Newfoundland. I hope that their interest will continue to grow. I feel both of these ministers have the welfare of Newfoundland at heart, and I hope that they will continue to give consideration to our fishermen who are working so hard and so long in an attempt to get a living. At the present time more than 30 per cent of the working class in Newfoundland are without employment, and I think that every assistance should be given them to earn a dollar which is so badly needed.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subtopic: REQUEST FOR ACTION TO AID FISHERMEN
speechtext:
listened with interest to the comments of the hon. members for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill), Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Granger) and Trinity-Conception (Mr. Tucker) with regard to the plight of the Newfoundland fishery, and more especially and what is perhaps of greater concern of us, the plight of the Newfoundland fishermen. This question is a complex one. It has been perplexing the governments down through the years. One has but to look briefly at the history of Newfoundland to see that the economy, up to perhaps a few years ago, was based solely on fish; it was a one-product economy. The folly of this economic condition became evident in Newfoundland during the world-wide depression in 1933, for at that time we found ourselves unable to sell our fish in the world markets. Of course, the results of that were catastrophic.
Now, I am one, sir, who is of the opinion that the future of Newfoundland, and to a very large extent the future of Canada's tenth province, will ultimately depend on the attitudes and policies of this government and the provincial government toward the fishery of Newfoundland. Whatever else can be said about industrialization, our forest resources and our mineral resources, the world will 66968-9-199i
Request for Aid to Fishermen always require food. As we all know, fish is a high protein food and fish is one thing we have in abundance in Newfoundland.
Without being partisan on this subject, Mr. Speaker, and I do not mean to be, although the temptation is great, I am reminded of the provincial election campaign in Newfoundland in 1951 when we heard much about industrialization; the great new factories, the growing industrialization; the great Latvian industrialist, and what have you.
At that time the Newfoundland premier went to the province to ask for a mandate for his industrialization program. One slogan used in that campaign was, "We will take
10,000	fishermen out of the fishing boats and put them into plants." This situation came about at a time when the Newfoundland fisherman, as a result of the prosperity of the second great war, was tending to get away from his fishing boat and to take more lucrative employment at United States bases in Newfoundland and other construction projects that had been started in the province as a result of union. This was hardly an encouragement to the fishermen of the day to go back to that industry which I maintain is our mainstay.
At one time there were several settlements in my constituency which were fishing headquarters, the most prosperous fishing communities in Newfoundland. The fisherman had his own cod trap and perhaps he had his own boat. He caught his fish and had his own plot of land in his backyard. He could supply himself with enough supplemental agricultural products to take care of his own needs over the winter and if he could get a good price for his fish he had a good year. In other words, the Newfoundland fisherman at that time was independent. He did not depend on unemployment insurance. He did not depend on family allowances. He did not depend on social security. He depended on his own sweat and toil, as did his forefathers, to get a living from the sea and he was a better man for it.
What do you find today if you go into these same settlements? You will find the little potato field grown over with weeds. He no longer keeps dairy cattle or poultry to supply his own needs. His fishing gear is rotting. His nets have rotted away and in some cases the people have not even bothered to request that the wharf be rebuilt. I maintain this is a sad plight for a region that was considered the fishing centre of the world. Perhaps the day will come again when Newfoundland can point with justifiable pride to its fishery and lead the world in that very important industry.
I support the views put forward by the three hon. members from Newfoundland who

Request for Aid to Fishermen sit opposite but I am sure they did not mean to suggest that the government will be able to pull a trick out of a magic hat and come up with the answer to this very complex problem. Having in mind the comments that have been made this evening and bearing in mind the unfortunate circumstance of the failure of the Newfoundland fishery last year, perhaps the result will be a reappraisal of what was at one time a great industry. We hope it will perhaps result in our taking a more realistic approach to this primary industry because in the final analysis, as has been suggested before, this is not a problem of economics but a human problem. It is a problem of whether or not a great number of Canadian citizens will be able to continue proudly the task of the fisherman as their forefathers did before them and as I am sure Newfoundland fishermen will do in years to come.

speechtext: Order. I am not sure whether the hon. member is coming to the subject by a roundabout method but it seems very roundabout. The grievance raised originally by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate had to do with the cod fishermen of Newfoundland and more specifically with the possibility of lending them money to help them restore their traps and gear. I am afraid I have allowed the discussion to range a little too broadly. This is not a general debate on fisheries nor on Newfoundland.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ACTION TO AID FISHERMEN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I was about to make my main point. We regret very much that when our cod fishermen on the west coast receive eight cents a pound Newfoundland fishermen only receive two cents a pound for the same kind of fish. It is our contention that one of the basic problems of the Newfoundland fishermen is their inability to help themselves. We feel that they have been exploited over the years by the fishing companies operating in that province. I know that certain ministers of the government have been very much concerned and have in their own way attempted to aid the fishermen of Newfoundland to help themselves and to organize in such a way that they will be masters of their own destiny. I only wondered at this point as to what the hon. members who had participated in this debate had done in years past to help the fishermen of Newfoundland to become masters of their own destiny and to bring them from the bondage of slavery which is now taking place, indeed which has always taken place, amongst the people who sold their souls to the company store, namely the fishing companies.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ACTION TO AID FISHERMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have often wondered if the people of Canada in general appreciate the value of fisheries to this country and sufficiently understand its trials and problems. In the first place, the fishing industry is one of our great export industries. It is worth $90 million to $100 million a year to our economy. Most of the fish which is caught and processed is sold abroad, chiefly throughout the eastern seaboard of the United States. It is an export industry which is growing very fast. I think it is safe to say that it is one of the brightest industries in the Atlantic provinces. It is modernizing itself every day. Costs are kept down in producing the product; and our fishermen are learning new techniques and advancing as fast as they can.
Before I go any further to discuss the matter raised by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill), I would like to take a moment to pay tribute to a group which I think is perhaps the most courageous of Canadians. They are both

courageous and self-reliant, and in two ways. First, they face a great physical hardship in earning their living. They leave the shore in small boats to go on the high seas to catch their product. Physically they are brave men and courageous. They are strong Canadians.
Secondy, in an economic sense I think it should be pointed out that our fishermen are amongst the most self-reliant and independent of Canadians. Other industries come before the government asking for tariff protection and other aid. In the case of the fishermen we have men who catch their product and put it on the markets of the world without help from anybody. The fisherman does not ask for tariff protection. He is prepared to keep his costs down and fight the battle on the straight basis of economic supply and demand. The fishermen whom I know on the Atlantic coast in my province, particularly in my own constituency, are men who bring their product to the shore, process it and put it on the markets of the United States in competition with every other nation.
Fish caught off the shores of my riding are processed at plants at Louisburg, Petit de Grat and Cheticamp and finds its way across the whole continent, even as far as Texas and to markets in Chicago.
There we have a prime example of a Canadian product being able to enter and compete in a foreign market without help. Again I say that I believe the fishermen, in the way their industry is growing and in their economic self-reliance, are an example to all Canadians. Look to the Canadian fisherman to see how we can pick up a market and expand an industry if we are ready to compete and meet another man's costs in order to put our products on the markets of the world.
I would like to digress for a moment and pay tribute to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) for the help he has given the fishing industry in my riding. My people feel that never before in our history has there been such co-operation from the Department of Public Works. Never before have we had such assistance to build much needed harbour facilities; for dredging and for many other things the fisherman needs in order to carry on his work. Again, I would like to join the other hon. members who have spoken in expressing my thanks to the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. MacLean) for the interest he takes in his department and for his closeness to the fishermen and their problems. It is a great tribute to him that on all sides of this house members rise in their places to congratulate him. We all appreciate his sincerity and tenacity in meeting the problems of the fishing industry.
28, 1959
Request for Aid to Fishermen
While the fisherman is certainly self-reliant and works hard, asking no quarter from anyone, he is a Canadian who has much less of life than many others. He is a man who takes great gambles. He takes gambles not only physically on the sea but also on his market. The great fluctuations in the price of fish and consequently in the income of the fisherman is a vital matter which should be faced by this house, and I think all members would like to see continuing attempts made to solve that problem.
In the past year we have seen, as other hon. members have mentioned, a great shortage of fish off the Atlantic coast, and as a result prices were high and for the catches which were brought to shore a good profit was available. But it is very common to see more fish caught and produced than the market can absorb. It is much more common to see low prices than sufficiently good prices, although we hope the future will show a general increase in prices as the market grows. But I would suggest that some more help be provided for the fishing industry in this respect; it would be of great value to this very important industry to effect greater stabilization of good market prices.
The fishing industry is unique in this respect, that there is really no large units of production in the industry. It is not carried on by large companies but by small companies and small units of fishermen, such as co-ops and others. The result is that there is no concerted, well organized attempt to advertise and to market fish on this continent. We are modernizing very fast our methods of catching and producing fish, but I feel there are many more things we could be doing in selling. I submit that one of our chief problems is too much competition among all these small companies which at times causes gluts on the market and great instability in price.
I think it would be very worthwhile and greatly appreciated by the fishermen of our Atlantic provinces if some effort were made by the government, under the benevolent guidance of the Minister of Fisheries, to bring together many of these small companies which are competing in the great United States market in a common selling program. The United States is our chief market for fish. These small companies might be brought into a joint advertising program whereby they would contribute to a special program, and with help by the government in the way of an advertising grant there would be great advantage in such a program. We all know that other industries, such as the appliance and automobile industries, plan more in respect to selling sometimes than they do in
3140	HOUSE OF
Request for Aid to Fishermen producing. Our problem in the fishing industry has been that we have neglected to properly sell our product. Oftentimes this important food product which should be much more widely used, does not find a sufficient market to absorb it. Over the years ahead I would suggest to the minister that he try to help organize the proper advertising and marketing of fish chiefly in the United States of America. At the same time, Mr. Speaker, I should note that the United States fisheries are also an important competitor in their home market, and it might be an example of how our two nations should work together in economic matters if leadership were provided by Canada to bring together not only Canadian but United States companies into an organization which would market fish and provide the joint market that there should be for this product.
Another problem which arises in my riding, and I am sure in many more as well, is that while we are developing fast into a modern and growing industry, while our dragger fleets are increasing, and modern fish plants are replacing the older system, we are in danger of neglecting that great body of fishermen who fish out from the shore in small boats. The inshore fisherman is being replaced by the dragger, and I have no doubt that in the years to come the industry will tend more and more toward larger boats and modern plants. At the same time there are in my riding a great number of inshore fishermen, and these men find that small draggers coming in, particularly at night, destroy or carry off their gear. The damage thus done to the inshore fisherman in a single night can be almost irreparable. I know that the minister is doing everything he can to meet this problem and preserve a proper balance between the inshore fishermen and the draggers. Every effort should be made to see that as the draggers and trawlers increase, the inshore fisherman is protected, because the latter does make a significant contribution toward the catching and marketing of fish and represents a most important sector of the economy.
In conclusion I wish to endorse warmly the remarks which have been made by other hon. members tonight. I hope that the country as a whole will appreciate the problems which the fishermen face and do all that can be done to help them in their job of catching and marketing a vital Canadian product in very difficult circumstances, and to help in bringing greater stability to the industry.

speechtext:
I intend to be very brief because this is a problem which I have very much in mind and I look forward to being able to discuss it
[Mr. MacLellan.l

further on my estimates. Besides I do not wish to talk at any length tonight and crowd out other hon. members who may have grievances to raise on other subjects.
However, I do wish to say that I myself, and everyone in the government, in addition to the officials of my department, are very much aware of the problem which existed in Newfoundland last year due to the failure of the catch. The effects are still being felt, especially on the northeast coast of Newfoundland. I may say, as has already been said tonight, that the problem is not merely an economic one; it is a humanitarian one, because in many of these outport settlements where the fishermen live there is no alternative employment available, and it is very difficult to provide any alternative employment since they are situated in a one-economy area where there is nothing else to which to turn. I do not have the figures with me, but I may say that the number of fishermen who were not qualified for unemployment insurance last winter was not by any means as high as most of us feared it might be. I think the percentage which qualified in the winter just past showed a decline of somewhere between 12 and 15 per cent. I realize, of course, that in some areas it was much worse, and I do not want to fall into the error of the statistician who was drowned in a lake, the average depth of which was two feet. I know there were some areas where the catch was a failure and where almost all the fishermen failed to qualify.
The government has endeavoured to play its share in relieving this situation by embarking on a program of stage building, the procurement of materials and the building of wharves. This work was carried on even through the winter as far as was possible under the weather conditions. Although this is of little assistance to fishermen who experienced a catch failure, we are continuing to provide salt assistance to help the fishermen who cure their cod and produce dry salt codfish.
As far as special loans to fishermen are concerned-loans to enable them to engage in the industry at a reasonable level-I may say that there have been times when the governments of the maritime provinces-two of them, at least-have approached the federal government in a similar situation where the fishermen had had quantities of gear destroyed by storms. The two levels of government did, between them, make loans to fishermen in certain circumstances. This was some years ago, and I may say that the federal government of that day had a somewhat unhappy experience because they found that the recipients of the loans looked upon

them as grants, and in many cases they were never repaid. Those who did repay the loans looked upon themselves as having been gypped, and felt that honesty was not the best policy. I mention this only so that the house should realize that the problem is not a simple one. It is a very thorny one indeed. I do not want to say more at the present time except that, of course, as hon. members are aware, the Fishermen's Loan Act is in operation and there are some cases where that act might meet the needs of the fishermen involved.

Answer by: Hon. Michael Starr (Minister of
Labour):
Counts of claimants currently reporting are made at the end of each month only.
It is not possible to separate those who are qualified from those who are not because there are always a number of claims in process whose qualification or otherwise cannot be determined until the processing is completed.
The following figures, therefore, represent the number of claimants currently reporting at the Galt local office as at 31 March in each of the years shown:
1.	Total claimants reporting; (a) 1503; (b) 2489.
